problem: Embodied AI research is scattered across vision, language, RL and simulation, and mostly trained in isolation on static Internet-AI datasets. There is no concise overview that connects it to smart-city agents.
motivation: Smart cities rely on robots and intelligent agents that must see, talk, navigate, interact and reason. Learning through interaction, as in the Held & Hein kitten carousel experiment, is argued to be essential for real intelligence, so a compact map of the field, its tools and its open challenges is useful to newcomers.
key_idea: A concise narrative review that defines Embodied AI, breaks it into sub-fields (language grounding, VQA, embodied recognition, EQA, IQA, multi-agent systems), surveys simulators (MINOS, Habitat), and outlines future directions.
insight: The review's main takeaway is that fast simulators shift the field from static datasets to interactive training. Its one quantitative point, taken from the Habitat paper, is that PPO agents trained for 75M steps instead of 5M eventually outperform ORB-SLAM on PointGoal navigation, which the review credits to Habitat's speed of up to 10,000 fps. It also reports that depth-only agents generalize best across datasets and that RGB-only agents perform about as badly as blind agents. These are secondhand claims, and the paper runs no experiments or ablations of its own.
method: Definition and history: Traces the shift from Internet AI to embodiment from the mid-1980s, citing Brooks' insect-robot argument and the kitten carousel experiment.
Task taxonomy: Covers language grounding, language+vision (captioning, VQA, VQA with OCR), embodied visual recognition (active recognition, ShapeCodes, audio), EQA, IQA and multi-agent systems.
Navigation task definitions: Defines PointGoal, ObjectGoal and RoomGoal navigation, all without a ground-truth map.
Simulator review: Compares House3D, AI2-THOR, Gibson, CHALET, MINOS and Habitat by frame rate and configurability, focusing on MINOS and Habitat.
Benchmark summaries: Recaps MINOS baselines (Feedforward A3C, LSTM A3C, UNREAL, DFP) and Habitat baselines (PPO with different sensors vs ORB-SLAM2, measured by SPL).
Future directions: Discusses higher intelligence (qualia, artificial muscles and skin) and evolution of embodiment and sensors.

setting.simulator: n/a (reviews MINOS, Habitat, AI2-THOR, Gibson, House3D, CHALET)

numbers_note: Review paper with no experiments of its own; the only figures quoted (Habitat fps, PPO 75M vs 5M steps) are from other papers.
results: There are no original results. The review compiles findings from prior work: UNREAL beats other agents in large environments, DFP does better in small ones, and PPO trained for 75M steps eventually outperforms the ORB-SLAM2 pipeline on Habitat PointGoal navigation.
limitations: Selective, opinion-based coverage. The authors say each section is abstract and reflects their personal views.
Narrow simulator and navigation coverage: mainly MINOS and Habitat, PointGoal/ObjectGoal/RoomGoal, and no vision-language navigation (VLN) or quantitative comparison tables.
Loose link to smart cities: the introduction motivates smart cities, but the body rarely discusses city-scale applications.
